summary: A 1977 Telnet option for byte macros, which let one side send a short code that stands for a longer string of characters. It was replaced by RFC 735.

plainLanguage.summary: A shortcut key that types a whole sentence. This option lets a computer send a short code instead of long text.

subtitle: A Telnet option that lets one side send a single byte standing in for a longer string, to cut control overhead.

tldr.problem: Telnet subcommands need at least five characters on the wire, which is too much overhead when the data comes in small blocks.
tldr.mechanism: After negotiating the BM option, the sender defines a single macro byte that stands for a longer expansion string, and the receiver acts as if the full string had arrived.
tldr.outcome: The option is a simple data compression technique. It was replaced by RFC 735.

today: RFC 729 has been obsoleted by RFC 735, so it is not the current definition of this option.

sections.title: Why a Byte Macro Option
sections.content:
Subcommands for Telnet options need a minimum of five characters on the network: IAC SB, the option name, IAC SE. That is fine for rare subcommands but costly for block-oriented data, where a block separator might be needed after every five or ten bytes.

The BM option, option code 19, is meant as a simple data compression technique that removes this overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: If every tiny note needed a big envelope, most of what you mail would be envelope. This option lets you use a tiny code instead.

sections.title: Negotiating the Option
sections.content:
The option is enabled with the standard Telnet option negotiation. The side that sends IAC WILL BM is the sender of data and may define mappings between single bytes and longer strings. IAC WON'T BM and IAC DON'T BM refuse. The default is WON'T BM and DON'T BM, so no reinterpretation of data is allowed.

Apart from a blanket refusal, the receiver has no control over which mappings the sender defines.
sections.plainLanguage: First both sides agree to use shortcuts. Until they agree, everything is spelled out in full.

sections.title: Defining and Using Macro Bytes
sections.content:
The sender uses IAC SB BM DEFINE macro-byte count expansion IAC SE, where DEFINE is 1. The macro byte may be any byte except IAC (255). The receiver replies with ACCEPT (2) or REFUSE with a reason, BAD CHOICE (1) or TOO LONG (2). The sender must not use or redefine a macro byte until it has an answer.

After acceptance, each macro byte received outside a BM subcommand is treated exactly as if its expansion string had been received. Expanded strings are not reinterpreted, so recursive definitions cannot be made. A LITERAL subcommand marks a byte as real data. The text gives REFUSE and LITERAL the same value, 3. Bytes between 128 and 254 are recommended for macro bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: You say: from now on, the letter Q means 'please open the next page'. The other side says yes or says it cannot remember that. Then Q is all you need to send.
